clinicalPearls: Presents as sweating, flushing, and warmth over the pre-auricular and cheek skin triggered by eating, chewing, or even the anticipation of food
Most commonly develops months to years after parotid surgery (parotidectomy), but also follows parotid trauma, infection, or occurs congenitally in infants
The starch-iodine (Minor) test confirms and maps the affected skin by producing a colour change where gustatory sweating occurs
Symptoms range from a trivial curiosity to socially distressing sweating that soaks the cheek during meals
Botulinum toxin injected intradermally into the affected skin is the most effective and durable symptomatic treatment, blocking cholinergic sweat gland stimulation
Topical antiperspirants (aluminium chloride) and anticholinergic creams offer milder, shorter-lived relief
Meticulous surgical technique and interposition of tissue barriers at parotidectomy reduce the incidence
reference.pathophysiology: Frey syndrome arises from aberrant regeneration of severed parasympathetic secretomotor fibres that originally supplied the parotid gland. After injury (typically parotidectomy) these postganglionic parasympathetic fibres, carried with the auriculotemporal nerve, misdirect and reinnervate the denervated sweat glands and cutaneous blood vessels of the overlying facial skin. Because both pathways are cholinergic, a gustatory stimulus that would normally provoke salivation instead drives sweating and vasodilatation of the skin, producing localised gustatory sweating and flushing in the auriculotemporal distribution.
additionalDifferentials: Salivary fistula or sialocele after parotid surgery
additionalInvestigations: Minor starch-iodine test to demonstrate and delineate the sweating area
Clinical history correlating symptoms with eating and prior parotid surgery or trauma
Gravimetric or quantitative assessment of sweat production for research or treatment monitoring
Ultrasound of the parotid bed if a sialocele or recurrent mass is suspected
Photographic mapping before botulinum toxin treatment to guide injection sites
redFlags: A new mass in the parotid bed suggesting recurrent tumour rather than simple gustatory sweating
Systemic flushing with palpitations or hypertension suggesting a neuroendocrine cause
Signs of persistent salivary fistula or infection at the operative site
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often improves or stabilises over time; symptoms are reliably controlled with botulinum toxin, although repeat injections are needed as the effect wanes over several months to a year.
pitfalls: Confusing gustatory sweating with a salivary fistula or sialocele after parotidectomy
Failing to formally map the area with the starch-iodine test before botulinum toxin injection, leading to undertreatment
Overlooking congenital Frey syndrome in an infant with facial flushing during feeds
Attributing generalised sweating or systemic flushing to Frey syndrome and missing an endocrine cause
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Intradermal botulinum toxin injection to the affected skin as the most effective and durable treatment, blocking cholinergic stimulation of sweat glands, with repeat injections as the effect wanes
Topical antiperspirants containing aluminium chloride and topical anticholinergic preparations for milder symptoms
Mapping of the affected area with the starch-iodine (Minor) test to guide targeted botulinum toxin injection
Reassurance and explanation given the benign nature and tendency to stabilise over time
Consideration of a surgical interposition barrier technique for refractory or severe cases
Follow-up to reassess symptom control and time repeat treatment
